title: What are the three delivery semantics (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once), and what causes each?
shortTitle: The three delivery semantics in Kafka (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once)
keyPoints: At-most-once: each message is delivered zero or one time, so messages may be lost but never duplicated (commit offset before processing).
At-least-once: each message is delivered one or more times, so messages are never lost but may be duplicated (process then commit offset).
Exactly-once: each message is effectively processed once, with neither loss nor duplication (idempotent producer + transactions).
The delivery semantic is determined by when the consumer commits its offset relative to processing and the producer's acks and idempotence settings.
For most banking use cases, at-least-once with an idempotent consumer is the pragmatic and robust choice.
True exactly-once is native only to Kafka-to-Kafka flows; external side effects need application-level idempotency.

s1_definition.oneliner: At-most-once may lose but never duplicate, at-least-once may duplicate but never lose, and exactly-once does neither.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **At-most-once** – each message is delivered zero or one time; messages may be lost but are never duplicated, caused by committing the offset before processing or using `acks=0`.
- **At-least-once** – each message is delivered one or more times; messages are never lost but may be duplicated, caused by processing first and committing the offset afterward.
- **Exactly-once** – each message is effectively processed one and only one time, with neither loss nor duplication, achieved through idempotent producers and Kafka transactions.
- **Idempotent producer** – `enable.idempotence=true`, which makes the broker detect and discard duplicate sends from retries using producer id and sequence numbers.
- **Kafka transactions** – the ability to atomically write to multiple partitions and commit consumer offsets, so either everything commits or nothing does.
- **Idempotent consumer** – an application-level pattern where the consumer checks for duplicates (unique constraint, processed-id check) before applying side effects.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India mailing transaction receipts to Rajesh. At-most-once is like mailing a receipt and never following up: if the post loses it, Rajesh never gets it, but he never gets two. At-least-once is like mailing a receipt and re-sending if unsure it arrived: Rajesh definitely gets it, but he might receive duplicates. Exactly-once is a careful system where Rajesh gets the receipt once and only once, no matter what goes wrong.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Delivery Semantics: Offset Commit Timing
=========================================

At-Most-Once (commit BEFORE processing):
  Receive record -> Commit offset -> Process
                          │              │
                     CRASH HERE     Record LOST
                     (offset committed, processing skipped)

At-Least-Once (commit AFTER processing):
  Receive record -> Process -> Commit offset
                         │           │
                    CRASH HERE   Record REDELIVERED
                    (processed but offset not committed)

Exactly-Once (atomic transaction):
  Begin TX -> Process -> Write output + Commit offset -> Commit TX
                                                    │
                                               CRASH HERE
                                               TX aborted, nothing committed
                                               Restart: reprocess from old offset
                                               No duplicate output
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Delivery semantics describe how many times a message is processed when failures happen. At-most-once commits the offset before processing, so a crash loses the record. At-least-once processes first and commits afterward, so a crash causes redelivery and duplication. Exactly-once uses idempotent producers and Kafka transactions to ensure neither loss nor duplication, but only for Kafka-to-Kafka flows.

At National Bank of India, the choice depends on the data. Dashboard metrics use at-most-once because losing a few points is harmless and they refresh constantly. Transfer events use at-least-once with manual offset commits and an idempotent consumer keyed by transfer id, which gives effectively-once results so Rajesh is never double-debited. Kafka-to-Kafka enrichment pipelines use full exactly-once with transactions.

The crucial real-world caveat is that true exactly-once only covers Kafka-internal writes. When the side effect is a database or an external API, the Kafka transaction cannot include that external operation, so you still need application-level idempotency. This is why at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer is the pragmatic banking default.

Remember one sentence: at-least-once with an idempotent consumer is the banking default because it guarantees no loss while preventing duplicate effects through application-level deduplication.
